title: Transfer: Intersect Two Interval Lists
oneLiner: Two people's busy times, each sorted and non-overlapping. Return the times both are busy, in one pass with a pointer into each list.
keyTakeaway: Two intervals overlap exactly when the later start is not after the earlier end: max(starts) <= min(ends), and that range is the overlap. With both lists sorted, the interval that ends first can't overlap anything further along the other list, so advance its pointer.
explanation:
This follows Merge Intervals with an unfamiliar twist: instead of one list to combine, you get two lists a and b. Each is sorted by start and has no overlaps inside itself. Return every interval where they overlap, in order. Endpoints are inclusive, so [1, 5] and [5, 10] meet in [5, 5].

Comparing every interval of a with every interval of b works, at O(n x m). The sorted order gives a one pass method. Keep a pointer i into a and j into b. Look at a[i] and b[j]: their overlap, if any, runs from lo = max(a[i] start, b[j] start) to hi = min(a[i] end, b[j] end), and it exists when lo <= hi. That is the same overlap test Merge Intervals made after sorting, written for two intervals at once.

Then move on from whichever interval ends first. Say a[i] ends first. Every later interval of b starts after b[j] ends (b has no overlaps inside itself), and b[j] ends at or after a[i] does, so no later interval of b can reach back to a[i]: it has nothing more to meet, and i++. If they end at the same time, either can move. Each step advances one pointer, so the whole walk is O(n + m), and the output can hold up to n + m intervals.

The visualization intersects a = [[0, 2], [5, 10], [13, 23], [24, 25]] with b = [[1, 5], [8, 12], [15, 24], [25, 26]]. The cells are the intersections found so far.

Explain why the same idea works: before you move on, write two or three sentences on what this has in common with Merge Intervals. Where does the overlap test come from, what does sorted order let you throw away at each step, and why is it safe to advance the pointer of the interval that ends first?

recognitionSignals: Two (or more) sorted lists of ranges, and you need where they overlap, or where both or neither are busy.
"Common free time", "when are both available", or intersecting schedules.
gotchas: Use <= in the overlap test: touching endpoints overlap in a single point here.
Advance the interval that ends first, not the one that starts first, or a long interval in one list misses later partners.
Either list can be empty; the answer is then empty.
confusableWith: Merge Intervals combines overlapping intervals from ONE list into their union; this finds the intersection of TWO lists that are already sorted.
Linked List Pointers: Merge Two Sorted Lists uses the same two pointer walk over two sorted inputs, advancing whichever is smaller.

complexity.note: Each step advances one of the two pointers, so at most n + m steps. The output can hold up to n + m intervals; the walk itself needs O(1) extra.
